rows.synopsis: A game of tag leads to a curious discovery.
rows.situation: Duck and Goose find a big round thing in the meadow, decide a baby bird is inside, and take on the job of keeping it warm until it hatches, guarding it through rain and all their own squirming impatience.
rows.coping: They treat the job seriously: sitting patient watch, building a practice 'bird doll' to rehearse care, covering the egg in the rain. And when Bluebird reveals the 'egg' is really a ball, they don't grieve the game; they turn it into a welcome gift for Mama Duck's real new duckling.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: gentle imaginative play and care-giving rehearsal play squarely 2-4; the mistaken-identity reveal lands at every age. script_vs_synopsis: synopsis stops at 'a curious discovery'; the script carries a full caretaking arc (practice doll, rain rescue, ball-as-gift turn) and its refrain about different ideas fitting together.
rows.per_story_synopsis: A game of tag ends under a tree, where Duck and Goose find something big and round that they decide is very egg-like. A baby bird must be inside, so a pair of flightless birds does what it must: climb up, sit careful watch, and practice being parents on a homemade bird doll while they wait. When rain threatens the nest and Bluebird finally looks inside, the truth comes out: it's a ball. And a ball, it turns out, is exactly the right welcome gift for a brand-new duckling next door.

rows.synopsis: Duck and Goose meet up with Thistle and learn about what makes her unique.
rows.situation: A new bird, Thistle, crashes Duck's dandelion wish, blowing away the last gray dandelion in the patch. The trek to Fuzzy Field for more stalls when tall wildflowers block every view, and Duck nearly gives up on his wish.
rows.coping: Duck owns his letdown instead of sulking, and when Thistle blames herself for bumping the dandelion, he spots the fix inside the mistake: the flutter that caused the trouble can lift her high enough to spot the path. Her difference saves the trip, and the wish the friends finally make is that they stay best friends.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: wishing games and new-friend jitters play 2-4; the keep-changing-my-mind thread lands with 5-7 too. script_vs_synopsis: synopsis says the pals 'learn what makes her unique'; the script is more specific: Thistle's clumsiness costs Duck his wish, then the very same fluttering finds Fuzzy Field, and the wished-for prize (her waddling song) is hers. off-list consideration: 'excited' for story 1's waiting arc; 'happy' holds instead.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Thistle arrives the way she seems to do everything: by accident, at speed, right through Duck's last dandelion wish. An expedition to Fuzzy Field follows: through boulders, over leaves, past flowers grown too tall to see across. When Duck nearly calls the whole wish off, Thistle's fluttering turns out to be the one talent that can find the way. Three wishes close the day: friendship, one perfect day, and a waddling song.

rows.episode_title: Go to the Beach / Measuring Tree
rows.synopsis: Duck convinces Goose to take a trip to the beach.
rows.situation: Duck is bored with the same old meadow and wants a first trip to the beach; Goose is sure everything new is too slimy, too pointy, or too sandy, and would rather stay where the grass is gorgeous.
rows.coping: Each friend gives the other's way a real try: Goose finds the seaweed gorgeously green up close, and Duck agrees to stay longer for Goose even while missing home, until a seashell that echoes like their brook gives him something to love. Meeting in the middle, not picking a winner.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: first-trip jitters and homesickness play 2-4; the meet-in-the-middle reciprocity lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis is a single line; the script shows the negotiation both ways (Duck tries staying for Goose after Goose tried the beach for Duck) and gives the payoff a concrete object, the shell that sounds like home.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Duck has worn out the meadow: pebbles found, forts built, stump danced on. He wants somewhere new. Goose wants nowhere but the gorgeous grass he knows. When Duck's 'pretty please' wins, Goose packs his doubts along and finds the slimy, pointy, sandy beach greener and gentler than advertised. Then Duck misses home before the day is done, so they trade: he tries loving the beach for Goose, and a shell that whispers like their brook settles the argument for both of them.

rows.episode_title: Go to the Beach / Measuring Tree
rows.synopsis: The duo find out how much they've grown and a disappointed Duck attempts to grow faster.
rows.situation: On measuring day Goose earns a new mark two inchworms higher, and Duck's mark doesn't move. Suddenly his perfectly good height feels wrong, and he'll try anything to grow before the next measure.
rows.coping: Goose helps him try every scheme (stretching, tiptoe practice, being planted and watered, yoga), and when each flops, they laugh at the flop instead of nursing it ('it made a tough situation funny'). The script's landing line does the real resolving: high or low on the tree, they're splendid just the way they are.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: growth-mark celebration plays 2-4; the size-comparison envy and the mound trick land 5-7. honesty note: Duck's 'higher mark' comes from standing on Gopher's dirt mound. The script plays it as celebration, but the stated moral is self-acceptance, and that line is the resolution we tag. script_vs_synopsis: synopsis gives the disappointment one clause; the script builds five escalating silly schemes and names the relief explicitly ('you're the best you there is').
rows.per_story_synopsis: Measuring day brings Goose two inchworms of good news, and Duck nothing new at all. His height, fine five minutes ago, suddenly feels like a problem to solve, and he solves it the Duck way: get stretched like rubber, wobble on tiptoes, get planted like a vegetable, watered, and folded into yoga. Nothing grows but the laughs. A gopher's dirt mound finally hands him the higher mark he wanted, along with the better prize: a pair of friends agreeing that high or low, they're splendid just as they are.

rows.synopsis: Duck and Goose learn the value of persistence while trying to build and fly a kite.
rows.situation: A runaway hat on a string inspires Duck and Goose to build a kite from scratch (paper, vines, sticks, a rubber ball, tree sap, and the hat itself), then get it to actually fly, one flop at a time.
rows.coping: They treat every failure as information: the knot untied gets retied tighter, the stuck-in-sap friend gets helped out, and the no-wind stall gets reimagined (wind is just moving air, so Goose runs against the breeze while Duck's rubber ball bounces the kite higher). Different ideas, same kite, finally aloft.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: build-and-flop comedy plays 2-4; the stepwise troubleshooting (knot, wind, lift) lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: synopsis says 'learn the value of persistence'; the script shows where persistence lives: three named failure modes (held too long, knot untied, no wind) and two different fixes merged at the end. The rock-stick-leaf who-flies-first ritual is script-only color.
rows.per_story_synopsis: A hat that refuses to be caught gives Duck and Goose a better idea: a kite. They build one out of everything they have: Goose's precious un-wrinkled paper, saved vines, a rubber ball for bounce, sticky tree sap and all. The launches fail the way first launches do: released too soon, knotted too loose, stalled by a windless sky. Then Goose runs into the wind, Duck bounces the ball, and the sort-of-almost-flying kite becomes a flying one.

rows.synopsis: After picking plums, they face a delivery dilemma.
rows.situation: Duck and Goose volunteer to pick plums for Bluebird's party, then spend the whole delivery nearly losing them: a dropped basket, a steep hill, and a final tumble that squashes every plum right before the party.
rows.coping: Goose carries the basket slow and careful while Duck races ahead to tell Bluebird, each taking the half of the job that fits him. The squashed plums become two treats instead of none (plum pudding plus plum juice), and the ground rule lands: it doesn't matter how they look, it matters how they taste.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: don't-drop-the-plums suspense plays 2-4; the looks-vs-taste reframe lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'delivery dilemma' in the synopsis is, in the script, a fast-versus-slow temperament clash that resolves by splitting the job, plus the squash-isn't-spoil turn, which the synopsis doesn't hint at.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Bluebird is throwing a treats-and-tweets party, and the treats need plums. Picking them is easy; delivering them is the epic: a basket chased downhill, a hill climbed one careful waddle at a time, and a last-second tumble that squashes the whole harvest. With guests arriving, Duck and Goose salvage the day by squashing on purpose: plum pudding from one friend, plum juice from the other, and a party none the wiser about how close the treats came to disaster.

rows.synopsis: On a trip to find the shiniest rock, Duck and Goose discover all of the fun within the forest.
rows.situation: A treasure hunt for the shiniest rock in the meadow derails when Duck chases a frog and skips the mud puddle, leaving Bluebird's path, and the two friends are well and truly lost in the forest.
rows.coping: Goose backtracks by remembering every silly thing Duck did along the way, and Duck's stump-dancing and joke-telling keep the lost part from feeling scary; a butterfly heading toward sunny flowers points them out of the trees. The detour's delights get named as discoveries, not wasted time.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: getting-lost reassurance plays 2-4; the backtrack-by-memory navigation is a nice stretch for 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'all of the fun within the forest' is Goose's noticing plus Duck's game-making in the script, and the hunt ends on a double reveal, a kinda-shiny kinda-small rock first and the truly shiniest one after, which the synopsis flattens.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Bluebird has found the shiniest, purpliest rock in the whole meadow, and Duck and Goose want it. Directions are given (stay on the path), and promptly un-given: a frog is followed, a puddle is skirted, and the meadow quietly becomes a forest. Lost but not done, the pair turns the detour into the destination: stump dance floors, honey-sweet blooms, jokes retold, until remembering exactly where the silly things happened walks them back to the path, and the rock gets its sparkle back.

rows.synopsis: A happy accident inspires a special birthday gift for Thistle.
rows.situation: Thistle's all-green birthday party needs a present, and Duck and Goose decide to make one: a painting. Then their favorite colors clash, the friends split up to paint apart, and Duck smears his picture by rushing back too soon.
rows.coping: Duck owns the rush-job mistake instead of hiding it, both admit painting apart was no fun, and when the two small paintings leave an empty middle, Duck's paint-stomp dancing stumbles into the answer: blue mixed with yellow makes green, Thistle's favorite color, and the clashing colors make the gift together.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: gift-making and color play are 2-4; the separate-ways sadness and the color-mixing reveal stretch to 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis's 'happy accident' is two accidents in the script (the smeared rush-job painting and the paint-stomp footprints), with a real low point (missed friendship, ruined picture) the synopsis skips.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Thistle's birthday party will be green, from balloons to hats to cake to the greenest grass in the meadow, so a homemade picture seems like the perfect gift. It starts a color war: Duck paints blue, Goose paints yellow, neither likes how they meet, so they split up to paint alone. Alone turns out lonely, and a rushed return smears one painting into a smooshy mess. Then dancing feet stomp right through the puddles of paint, leaving green, and blue plus yellow finally makes the picture together.

rows.synopsis: Duck and Goose get a catchy tune stuck in their heads.
rows.situation: Bluebird's little tune worms into both friends' heads and wrecks everything they try: cloud counting falls apart mid-number, hide-and-seek gives Goose away, and even patty-cake dissolves into humming. The song will not leave.
rows.coping: They try force (headstand draining, shouting the song away) and avoidance (sleep, playing something else); all fail. Then they go ask Bluebird herself, and the fix is creation, not eviction: making up their own louder, sillier song finally pushes the old one out. Bonus honesty for parents: the closing gag has Bluebird catching their quack song. Earworms circulate.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: pure 2-4 slapstick earworm play. script_vs_synopsis: synopsis is a premise; the script is a catalog of failed fixes with a lesson about which strategy actually works (make something new rather than fight the thought), plus the circular ending the synopsis can't show. vocabulary note: 'earworm/obsession' has no approved situation tag, so it is written as own wording per guide.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Bluebird sings two bars of a little tune, and by lunchtime Duck and Goose can't count clouds, win at hide-and-seek, or finish patty-cake without drifting into 'beep bop, tweedle top.' They fight the song loudly, drain it gently, and sleep on it, and it only spreads. The cure, it turns out, isn't silence or force but a bigger, sillier song of their own, which evicts the old one and promptly takes up residence in Bluebird's head instead.

rows.synopsis: When a toy goes missing, they learn they have different approaches to tidying up.
rows.situation: Bluebird leaves her favorite toy, Earl the Squirrel, in their care while she picks berries. Between Goose's careful list and Duck's play-first impulses, the playhouse gets built, Earl gets played with, and then Earl vanishes minutes before Bluebird returns.
rows.coping: No time for a blame spiral: they think like a toy squirrel, reason that a squirrel wants a snack, and find Earl stuck in the superduper seed feeder, where Goose's gentle touch frees him without breaking it. Bluebird comes home to a mess and calls it beautiful.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: 2-4 throughout; the list-versus-play tension is a tidy-up routine parents will recognize. script_vs_synopsis: synopsis hands the lesson to tidying styles; the script's engine is borrowed-toy responsibility: the mutual blame beat ('you had him last') and the pretend-play search that finds Earl are script-only, and the rescue depends on Goose's deliberate gentleness with a 'delicate' machine.
rows.per_story_synopsis: A new playhouse needs one thing before the friends can play in it: everything on Goose's list. Crayons boxed, shells sorted, snacks staged, with Duck's heart pulling hard toward play the whole time, especially once Earl the Squirrel arrives to stay. Then a rubber ball, a flinch, and Earl is gone right as Bluebird's voice comes up the path. A squirrel-shaped search ends at the seed feeder, where patience and a gentle touch bring the favorite toy home safely, list or no list.

rows.synopsis: Determined to see their first sunrise, the pals try to stay awake all night.
rows.situation: Dark ends the hide-and-seek game, and it plants a worry in Duck: what if the sun doesn't come up tomorrow? The fix is to test the promise: stay up all night on the hill and watch the sunrise themselves.
rows.coping: Goose's reassurance ('the sun always comes up') becomes a plan, and when sleepiness keeps winning (songs and dancing backfire), they recruit the night itself as an ally: the bullfrog's bouncy beat and the fireflies' little lights keep their eyes open until the big light arrives, right on schedule.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: the sun-might-not-rise worry and the night-noise reframing sit at the heart of 2-4 bedtime experience. script_vs_synopsis: synopsis gives determination; the script gives the worry that motivates it ('what if the sun doesn't come up?'), a good-sleep concession ('just this once'), and the device of turning the night's own sounds and lights into wake-up helpers.
rows.per_story_synopsis: When darkness ends their game early, Duck asks the question every child has asked: what if the sun doesn't come up? Goose knows it always does, but knowing isn't the same as seeing, so the two build a scratchy-leaf-and-flower-fluff nest on the hill and commit to staying awake until morning. Sleep fights dirty: songs go droopy, dancing goes droopier. Then the night starts helping: a bullfrog's beat to bounce to, fireflies to watch, and the sun comes up exactly like Goose promised, greeted by the two first friends awake to say so.

rows.synopsis: Bluebird's talent for magic motivates Duck and Goose.
rows.situation: Bluebird's show (rabbit, carrot, seeds-to-gold) convinces Duck and Goose they can learn magic, but her lesson is a day away, and waiting until tomorrow is not in Duck's repertoire. Every self-taught attempt flops: no rabbit, no carrot, stubbornly brown seeds.
rows.coping: They build the missing pieces themselves (pizzazz wands, star-painted and self-designed wizard hats, homemade magic words) and keep trying new places when the trick keeps failing. The payoff needs patience they didn't plan: overnight, every tossed seed has bloomed into a gold flower. Their magic worked; it just worked on flower time.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: 2-4 dress-up magic play; the delayed-payoff structure reads 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'motivates' undersells the plot: the script is an impatience arc (lesson is tomorrow, they try tonight) whose twist is that the failed magic succeeds overnight, a payoff the synopsis doesn't mention at all. Bluebird's 'maybe you should be teaching me' is the pride beat the tag leans on.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Bluebird pulls a rabbit from a hat, a carrot from thin air, and gold from plain brown seeds, and declares that magic takes creativity and pizzazz, two things Duck and Goose have in spades. Her lesson starts tomorrow. Tonight, obviously. Wand sticks are borrowed from a very agreeable beaver, wizard hats are barked and berry-painted, and magic words go full hippopotamus-toes. Nothing turns to gold. Then morning comes, and every place they tossed those seeds is blooming gold flowers, and the students find out their magic worked all along.

rows.episode_title: Go Trick or Treating / Three-Legged Race
rows.synopsis: A quest for sweets turns spooky when Duck and Goose catch wind of a local “swamp monster.”
rows.situation: Costume negotiations end in a mutual surprise (a sheet ghost and a caped 'Great Gooster'), then Squirrel warns of a swamp monster after their treats, and Goose wants to skip Halloween and hide until Thanksgiving.
rows.coping: Goose says the worry out loud ('anything with monster in its name worries me') instead of swallowing it; Duck's superhero costume becomes his courage, facing the footprints and the stink rather than hiding, and the reveal does the rest: the 'monster' is Thistle, slimed on purpose, wanting to trick-or-treat with them.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: monster-rumor Halloween worry is core 2-4; the costume-compromise gag lands across bands. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis stops at the spooky wind; the script adds the hide-or-face decision as the actual climax, the treat-sharing rule ('save plenty for the party'), and the friend-behind-the-monster reveal.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Halloween needs two costumes, and Duck and Goose want two different Halloweens: rainbow elegance versus eight-armed excitement. They settle on surprising each other: Duck as a spooky ghost, Goose as the meadow's bravest superhero. Then Squirrel delivers a rumor: a swamp monster is after their treats. Goose measures the doorways for hiding; the Great Gooster plants his feet instead, and the monster hunt ends the best way rumors can: in a friend, covered in swamp slime, who just wanted to trick-or-treat along.

rows.episode_title: Go Trick or Treating / Three-Legged Race
rows.synopsis: A race between friends hits an unexpected snag.
rows.situation: Duck and Goose tie their inside legs together for their first three-legged race against Bluebird and Thistle, with Goose's safety knots tied so tight and so many that every step is a negotiation, and the two runners can't agree on fast or slow, splash or leap.
rows.coping: They build a rhythm ('move your inside foot on three'), split the mud problem the 'you be you' way, and when Bluebird and Thistle stop mid-race, they abandon their own finish to hop-and-tumble to the rescue. The friends were only fixing a snapped vine, and the pairs end trading techniques and crossing in a tie.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: tied-together slapstick plays 2-4; the rhythm-planning and rescue-over-winning logic land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the 'unexpected snag' of the synopsis is, in the script, Goose's over-engineered safety knots plus a pace mismatch, and the resolution includes a misread rescue and a technique swap, neither hinted in the synopsis.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Bluebird and Thistle are racing tied together (three legs, in step, smiling), and Duck and Goose want in. Goose ties the vine with every knot he owns, and suddenly the fastest friends in the meadow can't take a single step in step. Tumbles happen. Mud happens, differently, to each of them. Then the other pair stops dead in the woods, and winning stops mattering: over the tree, through the dizziness, as fast as three legs can go, to find a snapped vine, a spare, and two friends who'd love to learn the tumbly spin.

rows.synopsis: Duck and Goose plan for fun in a winter wonderland.
rows.situation: First snow of the season, and the two friends want opposite days: Duck wants exciting (snowball fights, ice-skating), Goose wants peaceful (footprint patterns, frost-gazing). Everything one loves, the other bounces off.
rows.coping: They split for a while, each doing their own thing, until Goose reframes sledding as both at once: zippy and zoomy for Duck, peaceful scenery-sitting for Goose. The sleds are Goose's beloved leaf collection, sacrificed to the hill, and the game they find fits both friends exactly.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: 2-4 snow play; the both-at-once synthesis is a nice 5-7 stretch. script_vs_synopsis: 'plan for fun' hides the actual structure: an excitement-versus-peace clash, a snow-duck compromise that still leaves Duck restless, and the sledding synthesis plus leaf-collection sacrifice, none of which the synopsis hints at.
rows.per_story_synopsis: The first snow turns the meadow into two different playgrounds: for Goose, a hush of footprints and frosty branches; for Duck, an arena. Snowball fights tire Goose out, skating rattles him, and a gentlemanly snow duck only holds Duck's attention so long. Then Goose flips his own rule: sitting still on a sled watching the world blur by is the most peaceful excitement there is, and Duck's friend's leafy collection becomes the fastest sled the hill has ever seen.

rows.synopsis: The pals work hard to help a lonesome flower bloom in the meadow.
rows.situation: A lone flower bud, Buddy, won't bloom, and every cheer-up attempt fails: hugs, silly dancing, even Goose's own scarf against the wind. He only droops further.
rows.coping: Goose's flower-smelling habit stops Duck mid-stride at an uprooted flower (Rooty), and the sight cracks the mystery: Buddy isn't sad for no reason, he's lonely. Replanting Rooty beside him takes teamwork (Duck digging fast, Goose tucking roots in gently), and the bloom comes overnight, on the flower's own schedule, two neighbors waking up together.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: 2-4 throughout; the loneliness diagnosis and wait-for-the-bloom patience read 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: synopsis says lonesome up front; the script earns it: three failed cheer-ups, the uprooted-Rooty discovery that names the feeling, and patience as the actual cure rather than any single gesture.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Between throws of the zig-zag-long-gone, Goose finds a flower bud all by itself in the meadow. Buddy won't bloom, and the friends throw everything at it: a big hug, tail-feather dancing, a scarf against the wind. Buddy droops on. Then Goose's habit of stopping to smell the flowers finds Rooty, an uprooted neighbor, and the mystery solves itself: Buddy needed company, not tricks. One fast dig and one gentle tuck-in later, two flowers sleep side by side and wake up blooming: one yellow, one white, just like their gardeners.

rows.synopsis: When Thistle gets upset with her new neighbor, Bluebird recalls the bumpy days of Duck and Goose's early friendship.
rows.situation: Thistle is feuding with the porcupine who just moved in upstairs, all falling sticks and a borrowed twisty twig, and declares friendship impossible before hello. Bluebird answers with the true story of how Duck and Goose started: an argument over a favorite hat that lasted a whole stormy day.
rows.coping: The story is honest about what didn't happen: no instant apology: they argued all day while a storm wrecked both nests. What heals it is doing: Duck's joke breaks the silence, they rebuild each other's nests the way the other likes, and Goose returns the hat cleaned, with a spare as a gift. In the frame, Porcupine apologizes for yelling, admits she's shy, and Thistle asks her to pick plums together.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: nest-vs-twig messiness plays 2-4; the flashback structure, the day-long grudge and the two-layer apology land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'bumpy days' is made concrete: the hat misunderstanding, the did-too/did-not day, the storm that finally interrupts it, and the fence Goose planned that neither ends up wanting. single-story episode (no segment split); script basis: full 22-min special.
rows.per_story_synopsis: A new porcupine upstairs, a shower of falling sticks, and Thistle has decided: friendship with this neighbor is impossible. Bluebird knows better, because she watched it happen: the day Duck wrecked a tidy nest, borrowed a hat by accident, and spent the afternoon in a did-too, did-not argument with the neatest bird in the meadow. It took a storm to stop them, two rebuilt nests to mend them, and one very clean hat to start a friendship that's still going, one you-be-you at a time. Upstairs, a shy porcupine gets her turn to say sorry, and the plums get picked together.

rows.synopsis: Duck encourages Goose to step out of his comfort zone.
rows.situation: Follow-the-leader is the bestie-best game ever, until Duck's quack-cident hurts his foot with the whole meadow arriving to play, and the only leader left is Goose, who has never once wanted the job ('I like to take my time to think').
rows.coping: Duck's reframe does the heavy lifting ('you don't have to lead like I do, you can lead like you do'), and Goose's offer of borrowed ideas gets gently declined. His thinking-slow pace becomes the game ('how slow can you go?'), and the friend who never leads leads the whole meadow, his way.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: follow-the-leader slapstick is 2-4; the lead-like-you confidence arc lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: synopsis says 'encourages'; the script forces the moment (an injury benches the usual leader), shows Goose asking for a scaffold and being told his own ideas are enough, and lets his tempo become the feature, a confidence arc the one-liner only gestures at.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Duck is the undisputed king of follow-the-leader, all action-y ideas and somersaults and crab walks, and Goose is its happiest follower. Then a moss-slide quack-cident benches Duck just as the whole meadow shows up to play. Goose pleads his case (he thinks too slow, he's not action-y), but 'lead like you do' turns out to be the best idea of the day: slow-motion leading, tippy-toes, a very silly dance, and a whirlwind finish that proves the goosiest leader is exactly what the game needed.

rows.synopsis: During a game of hide-and-seek, the friends lose sight of their shadows.
rows.situation: Hide-and-seek has gone stale: Goose always hides with his comfy blankie, Duck always with the ladybugs. So they invite their shadows to play. The shadows find them instantly, then vanish entirely as the sun goes down, and the friends decide the shadows must be afraid of the dark.
rows.coping: They treat the shadows' fear exactly the way they treat their own: Goose's firefly lantern makes the dark 'not so dark,' and Duck holds up his comfy blankie in the light so the shadows can see it's warm and safe. The shadows come back at the first glow, the fireflies stay on as a night-light, and good-nights get said to everyone, including two shadows.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: fear-of-the-dark is the core 2-4 situation; the projection move (worry about the shadows instead of themselves) is a gentle 5-7 discussion starter. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis says the friends 'lose sight of their shadows'; the script times it to sunset, builds the fear-of-the-dark reading, and lands a comfort-object-and-lantern bedtime resolution with a snoring punchline.
rows.per_story_synopsis: The greatest game in the meadow has a flaw: everyone knows everyone's hiding spot. The fix has four legs and follows them around: invite the shadows to play. The shadows are suspiciously good at hide-and-seek, then refuse to come out at all once the sun sets. The friends settle on a diagnosis nobody dares claim for themselves: the shadows are afraid of the dark. Firefly lantern, comfy blankie held high, and one by one the shadows come home, staying just long enough for good-nights, a night-light, and one last snoring question.

rows.synopsis: Hoping to cheer up Thistle, Duck and Goose plan a creative surprise.
rows.situation: Thistle has hurt her foot and can't come to the beach, and carrying her there fails half a meadow in. So the friends flip the plan: if Thistle can't come to the beach, the beach will come to the pond.
rows.coping: They interview Thistle about what she actually loves (the waves), then build the beach around her answers: gentle waves and splashy-crashy ones, surfing on a carried log, seagull pecking impressions, and a full seaweed underwater with fish, shark, and a two-bird octopus. Her verdict: not exactly the real beach. Even better.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: 2-4 imaginative play; the ask-what-they-love-first move is a 5-7 takeaway. script_vs_synopsis: 'creative surprise' undersells the engineering: the script includes the failed carry, the you-decide-what-you-love interview that steers the build, and the better-than-the-real-thing verdict.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Beach day has one problem: Thistle, benched by a hurt foot, watching from the meadow. Carrying her the whole way fails: the beach, it turns out, is farther than a duck thinks. So the beach relocates: waves whipped up pond-style (gentle for Goose's taste, splashy for Thistle's), surfing atop a log, and a seaweed-and-imagination deep sea with a fearsome shark and a very polite two-bird octopus. When Thistle surfaces from underwater, she delivers the review that ends the argument: it's not exactly the real beach. It's even better.

rows.synopsis: The duo helps a skunk manage her not-so-charming stink clouds.
rows.situation: Skunk, brand-new to the meadow, has been playing Duck, Duck, Goose all alone, with pinecones named Duck. She sprays whenever she's surprised, and every new arrival at the big game is another chance for the stink to scare the friends away.
rows.coping: The friends co-design a warning system: Duck calls ahead that he'll yell, Goose announces anyone approaching ('please state your name'), and when Skunk sprays mid-game anyway, nobody leaves: the friends just air out and come back. The payoff is Skunk tapped as the goose, chased, and safe at home plate with new friends all around.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: stink jokes and chase play are 2-4; the warning-system co-design and forgive-and-return beat land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'manage her stink clouds' is, in the script, a social problem: surprise-triggered spraying handled by advance warnings plus a community that returns after the smell; her lonely pinecone games are script-only context. vocabulary note: Skunk's spray reads as body-based embarrassment, covered by the ratified shame/embarrassment tag.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Skunk is new, shy, and stuck playing her favorite game with pinecones, because when she's surprised, she sprays, and the stink tends to send playmates running. Duck and Goose fix it the friend way: warnings before loud calls, name-stating at the edge of the woods, Goose on lookout duty. The system isn't perfect, and a spray still clears the field once, but everyone comes back when the air does, and the day ends with the one thing Skunk never got playing solo: tapped as the goose, chased at full speed, and safe in her own spot.

rows.synopsis: The friends cross paths with a struggling giant.
rows.situation: A game of hide-and-seek turns up a moving tree. Actually Moose, one antler snagged in the willow, resigned to standing there forever. Getting to his head means fluttering too high, climbing too slow, and riding a ticklish, wiggly hump.
rows.coping: The rescue almost ends twice: the vines only tighten when everyone pulls, and Moose is ready to settle in. The turn is Goose's counterintuitive insight, relax and keep it loose, which loosens the vines enough for patient, knot-by-knot untying, with one last flutter for the knot nobody can reach. Moose's exit line flips his own forecast: forever wasn't as long as he thought.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: giant-climbing slapstick plays 2-4; the calm-loosens-the-vines device and Moose's given-up talk ('I guess I might as well get used to it') give 5-7 a real lesson about helplessness. script_vs_synopsis: 'cross paths with a struggling giant' hides that the struggle is partly emotional: Moose talks like someone who's stopped expecting rescue, and the script makes calmness itself the rescue technique.
rows.per_story_synopsis: The tree trunk moves. The trees moo. And it turns out the biggest tree in the willow patch is Moose, with an antler caught fast and a plan to stand there forever. Duck and Goose will not allow it. The climb up their new friend is an expedition of vines swung on and a hump mistaken for a mountain and ridden like a slide, and the rescue gets harder before it gets better: pulling tightens the tangle, and only loosening up, in body and in hope, unwinds it knot by knot.

rows.synopsis: Duck and Goose attempt to save a teeny-tiny community.
rows.situation: A line of ants hauling one enormous grape is caught in the rain, swept off course, separated from their hill, and floating downstream with their breakfast, lunch and dinner heading the wrong way.
rows.coping: Four rescues, each built on the last: a rock-and-pinecone dam that at least redirects the river, a rock stepping-stone bridge over the mud, one more rock to bend the water away, and finally Goose's pinecone 'ant floaties': the too-floaty mistake from the first dam becomes the ride home. Refusing to quit is the stated engine: those ants should never give up, and neither should we.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: 2-4 rescue-cheering play; the failed-plan-repurposed logic (floaty pinecones, redirected river) lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'attempt to save' undersells the sequence: the script runs four distinct engineering attempts, including the dam's side effect being reframed as the win.
rows.per_story_synopsis: The ants have found the biggest grape in the meadow, and the meadow has found the biggest rainstorm. One by one the little line goes floating, grape and all. Duck and Goose answer with engineering: a dam of rocks and pinecones, a stepping-stone bridge, a river redirected by one well-placed rock, and when nothing quite finishes the job, the pinecones that floated too well become exactly the life rafts the ants need. Cheering optional, provided freely.

rows.synopsis: Inspired by an elegant trio, Duck and Goose stage a dance performance.
rows.situation: The swans dance beautifully, and at the same time. Duck and Goose promise their own show, then discover the hard part: each can't do the other's moves, and 'the swans make it look so easy' because swans are all alike, while the two of them are not alike at all.
rows.coping: After both imitations flop, they stop trying to be swans, or each other, and invent 'together-not-together': a two-act show with proper introductions, each friend doing the moves his own body loves. The swans love it, and the show's name is the lesson.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: warm-up-and-tumble slapstick plays 2-4; the comparison trap ('it's so easy for them') and the together-not-together resolution land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'inspired by an elegant trio' skips the whole middle: the failed mirroring, the named reason swans succeed where they can't, and the invention that resolves it.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Three swans glide across the pond dancing in perfect unison, and Duck and Goose promise their very own show. There's just one catch: Goose's smooth tap-steps won't fit Duck's feet, and Duck's rolls and spins leave Goose mucky and dizzy. The swans, they realize, are all alike, and the two of them never have been. So the performance becomes two shows in one: Goose's flap-tastic tap act, Duck's whirlwind spins, and a finale together-not-together that gets the elegant audience dancing too.

rows.synopsis: The pals try to uplift Bluebird with songs and treats.
rows.situation: Bluebird misses her morning song for the first time ever. She has the frownies and doesn't know how to fix them. Duck and Goose throw their whole toolbox at it, and every tool fails.
rows.coping: Nothing works: power breathing, a cheer-up song, a perfect plum, a puppet show, a whole parade of funny noises. The harder they try, the worse everyone feels. The rescue arrives sideways: Duck's own sadness gets soothed by one of Goose's hugs, which gives Duck the idea. They ask Bluebird first ('I really could use a hug'), and one group hug does what nothing else could. Presence and asking beat performing.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: 2-4 comfort language; the consensual-ask beat and the friends' own sadness spiral read 5-7. vocabulary note: the friends' failed-fixing feeling edges toward hopeless (ratified); 'sad, confused' chosen because the row's center is Bluebird's unexplained frownies; flag if a helplessness tag is wanted. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis's songs and treats are the failed strategies; the script's resolution is the group hug discovered by accident, which the synopsis omits entirely.
rows.per_story_synopsis: No morning song. Duck and Goose investigate, and find Bluebird in bed with the frownies, sad, grumpy, and no idea why. So they fix the unfixable: power breathing, a tune, the perfect plum, a puppet show, a parade of funny noises. Each attempt flops, and each flop weighs on the fixers, until Duck, frowning himself now, gets a Goose hug and feels it work. If a hug can help him, maybe Bluebird would like one. She would. The frownies lift, the song comes back, and the best way to start the day turns out to be asking, and hugging.

rows.synopsis: Duck and Goose help Rabbit see a dragonfly up close.
rows.situation: Rabbit has spotted a sparkly, buzzy zoom-thing too fast even for him, and he wants a real look. Getting close means being super-duper quiet, crossing the pond, where Rabbit is a slow swimmer, and building a raft that actually floats, sails, and moves.
rows.coping: Every setback gets a fix: the sinking raft gets retied tighter, the wind steals the sail so Goose paddles, leafy sticks become paddle pushers, and the smooth-slow versus zippy-fast clash resolves in the episode's best line: you don't need to paddle the same, you just need to paddle together.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: raft-building slapstick plays 2-4; the two-paddles-one-boat cooperation logic lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'help Rabbit see a dragonfly' hides the full engineering chain (raft, sail, paddles) and the quietness requirement that shapes every move; Rabbit's role as the guide-with-a-drawing is script-only.
rows.per_story_synopsis: There's a dragonfly over the pond, transparent rainbow wings and pizzazzy flying, and Rabbit has never seen one up close. Neither have Duck and Goose. The mission goes by raft: a test-run that sinks, sticks retied Goose's patient way, a leaf for a sail, and paddles improvised from leaves and sticks. When zippy-fast and smooth-slow paddling nearly capsize the project, Rabbit settles it, paddle each your own way together, and the raft glides within whispering distance of the most beautiful bug in the meadow.

rows.synopsis: Kindness leads to chaos while making snacks.
rows.situation: One shared granola bar for Squirrel becomes a bakery of special orders: strawberries, carrots, cashews (no, forget the cashews), Juneberries, extra honey, really-really-big cherries, until Duck is stuck in the honey and nobody can remember who wanted what.
rows.coping: When two chefs can't hold every order, Goose flips the problem: give every waiting friend a bowl and let them build their own bar. Duck turns the ingredient line into a musical parade, the friends get exactly what they wanted (including one changed mind about cashews), and the chaos ends as everyone's own creation.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). age band: 2-4 kitchen slapstick; the too-many-orders-to-hold overwhelm and self-serve fix read 5-7. vocabulary note: 'overwhelmed' is the honest word for the peak moment and is off-list; tagged confused, frustrated instead; flagging for the vocabulary review. script_vs_synopsis: 'kindness leads to chaos' is right about the cause and silent on the resolution: the let-everyone-make-their-own turn is script-only.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Duck and Goose bake granola bars together, one gooey gloppy rainbow and one beautifully blobby, and the meadow wants in. Then the special orders start: strawberries, carrots, raisins, no wait, cashews, Juneberries from behind the playhouse, the biggest bar ever, and a friend stuck up to the wings in honey. With two chefs, one brain between them, and a line of waiting friends, there's only one possible menu: everybody's kitchen now. Bowls for all, a musical line to the ingredients, and granola exactly the way each friend likes it.

rows.episode_title: Thistle's Quest for the Best / Beaver's Sticks
rows.synopsis: Thistle wants to find out what she's the best at.
rows.situation: Thistle says she's the best at so many things, but the bestest of all? She doesn't know. Duck and Goose volunteer to find out, testing leaf houses, castles, juggling, cloud-bouncing, hopping, drumming, logrolling, and stretching, with a Thistlelina tale getting taller between every try.
rows.coping: The trials are a montage of glorious failures (leaf-alanche, drums knocked over), and the answer arrives from watching what she does anyway: the friends realize the best story of all time just told itself: Thistle is the bestest storyteller. Her own gift was hiding in plain sight, narrating the search for it.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: build-it-and-bounce slapstick plays 2-4; the strengths-in-plain-sight resolution and the meta-trick (her talent visible in the telling) land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis names the quest; the script supplies the trial-and-failure montage, the nested Thistlelina epic (acorn house, moon-lassoing), and the discovery that the answer is the narrator herself.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Thistle is the best at fluttering, and juggling, and probably everything, but what is she bestest at? The friends put her through the trials: a leaf house that relaxes, a castle that avalanches, juggling that needs 'just a little more practice,' all while pausing for the legend of Thistlelina, the tiny duck who lassoed the moon. Then they notice something: the story they keep begging her to finish is the best one they've ever heard. Thistle's search ends where it started: with her telling it.

rows.episode_title: Thistle's Quest for the Best / Beaver's Sticks
rows.synopsis: Duck and Goose search for the perfect sticks to make their friends happy.
rows.situation: The friends happily share a mystery pile of perfect sticks, a stick-lophone for Bluebird and stilts for Thistle, then meet Beaver, the pile's actual owner, who needs every one to finish his house. Now they have to ask their friends for the gifts back.
rows.coping: They own it fast ('we didn't know they were your sticks'), and the friends hand them back graciously; then the pair repairs the loss with made-to-order replacements (a shaker-drum, a twig guitar), de-stilts Thistle from above, and joins the build, plugging Beaver's wall hole while Thistle spots from Duck's shoulders.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: stilt wobbles and mud play 2-4; the take-back-the-gift apology and generous repair sequence lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis's 'perfect sticks to make our friends happy' omits the whole problem: the gifts were given in error and had to be reclaimed, which is the story's emotional spine.
rows.per_story_synopsis: A pile of smooth, straight sticks is a parade for Duck and a pond-viewing frame for Goose, and soon a stick-lophone for Bluebird and a pair of tall stilts for Thistle. Then Beaver arrives looking for his house-building supply, and the friends face the trickiest kind of fix-up: asking friends to return gifts they never should have given. Bluebird hands hers back with a smile, Thistle needs a rescue off her stilts, and the day ends with replacement instruments, a plugged wall, and one proud beaver.

rows.synopsis: The friends discover Bear hibernating in the meadow.
rows.situation: Bear is asleep out in the cold, far from his cave, and the problem grows by the minute: they can't wake him (it's his winter nap), they can't move him (he's far too heavy), and both DIY caves (sticks and snow) collapse. The thinkers are all thunked out.
rows.coping: The fix arrives as an accident: Rabbit and Mouse, using Bear as a snow hill, prompt the flip: 'you can't slide on Bear, but you can slide Bear.' His stick roof becomes a sled, the push-count gets a go-on-four compromise, and leaning together steers him home. A failed plan turned inside out, plus more friends, solves it.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: winter slapstick and sled play 2-4; the accident-becomes-answer turn and the go-on-four negotiation land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'discover Bear hibernating' names the setup only; the script's spine is the two-failed-caves despair spiral and the sled rescue built from it.
rows.per_story_synopsis: A mysterious echo turns out to be Bear, fast asleep in the snow, and this isn't an ordinary nap, it's the all-winter kind. Waking him fails, moving him fails, and building him a cave fails twice. Then two friends arrive looking for a sledding hill, find one shaped exactly like Bear, and hand the rescue its answer: if you can't move a mountain of a bear, slide him: roof-sled, four-count push, everyone leaning together, straight into a cozy cave.

rows.synopsis: Duck and Goose help twin raccoons Kit and Cub stop arguing.
rows.situation: Kit and Cub argue about everything: berries, toadstools, a dancing leaf, dress-up versus basketball. They look exactly alike but like completely different things, and until today they had never once played together.
rows.coping: The coaching is concrete: take turns (Cub's idea, then Kit's), and when one idea can't win, combine them: bop-and-blow leaf keep-up, then 'Hats in the Hoop,' a brand-new game that is Cub's dress-up and Kit's basketball at the same time. The coda holds the line: berries eaten one at a time or in a bunch, both ways okay.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: leaf-bopping and hat play 2-4; the siblings-look-alike-but-like-different-things thread and the invent-a-game-that's-both-ours move land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis says 'stop arguing'; the script reframes it: arguing isn't banned, it's redirected into turn-taking and a game built from both sisters' ideas.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Mama Raccoon is off gathering berries, leaving twins Kit and Cub to their favorite sport: arguing. Along come Duck and Goose, who know this territory well. First tool, taking turns: Cub's hop-like-a-toad game, then Kit's counting. Second tool, better: when a dancing leaf causes a standoff, the game grows bops AND blows; when dress-up and basketball collide in the playhouse, the sisters invent Hats in the Hoop and score. By the time Mama is home, the only thing left to argue about is whether berries go one at a time or in a bunch, and even that has an answer now.

rows.synopsis: The pals try to move a boulder that lands between their nests.
rows.situation: A seesaw swap gone wrong (Duck's rock was far too light) launches a really big rock squarely between the two nests, and now the best friends can't see each other at naptime. Duck can't sleep without seeing Goose, and every workaround fails.
rows.coping: Pushing fails, pulling fails, napping in each other's nests fails for perfectly them-shaped reasons (too messy, too tidy), and the rock-top nap ends in a tumble. The winning idea is the machine that caused it all: the seesaw, with Goose bouncing the boulder away. Two little friends moved a great big rock.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: seesaw physics slapstick plays 2-4; Duck's 'I need to see you when I sleep' is a real attachment beat for 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis starts at the boulder; the script explains its origin, the failed nap swaps, and the seesaw finish.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Naptime side by side is the best part of the day, until Duck swaps a too-light rock onto the seesaw and sends a boulder bouncing straight between their nests. Pushing won't budge it, pulling won't budge it, and each friend's nest is un-sleepable in for the other. After one high-and-lumpy try on top of the rock itself, Duck spots the answer in his own playground: a seesaw, a very determined bounce, and goodbye, rock.

rows.synopsis: Duck and Goose hunt for the perfect autumn leaf.
rows.situation: Goose finds a leaf shaped exactly like him and Duck doing a wing-ding, then loses it into a huge pile. Duck pledges to give up leaf-jumping forever to help search, even though crispy piles are his favorite thing in autumn.
rows.coping: Four search styles fail in order: jump-scanning (too fast), wing-to-wing sorting (leaves everywhere), orange-only culling (pumpkin orange is not carrot orange), and a blindfolded Goose (no sorting at all). The synthesis wins: Duck jumps so thousands of leaves fly at once, and Goose scans them mid-air. Found it. The coda closes the sacrifice loop with flower fluff padding for Goose's own first jump.
rows.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: leaf-pile mayhem plays 2-4; Duck's kept pledge and the both-styles search synthesis land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'perfect autumn leaf' undersells the stakes: the leaf is a portrait of the friendship, Duck's sacrifice is explicit ('even if it means I never jump in another leaf pile'), and the ending restores jumping for both.
rows.per_story_synopsis: On the first day of autumn, Goose finds it: an orange leaf shaped precisely like two best friends doing a wing-ding. Then it flutters into the biggest leaf pile in the meadow, the kind Duck dreams about. A pledge is made (no more jumping, ever, if that's the price), and the search begins. Jumping is too fast, sorting too slow, orange-sorting too confusing, until the friends discover the answer was teamwork all along: one duck launches the pile sky-high, one goose inspects every flying leaf. The wing-ding leaf is found, and by the last page even Goose is jumping, flower fluff and all.
